web_evidence.title: Excerpt from White Oleander by Janet Fitch
web_evidence.note: A sustained Chapter 1 excerpt, reprinted with Little, Brown’s permission, has Astrid narrating her actions, perceptions, age, and relationship to her mother as “I” and “we.”

web_evidence.title: Back Roads, a Novel in Progress: A Creative Thesis
web_evidence.note: This University of Delaware master’s thesis discusses Astrid and White Oleander as influential narrative models; its critical preface says the protagonist tells her story, and its annotated bibliography explicitly identifies the novel as a first-person narrative covering Astrid’s full foster-home journey.

web_evidence.title: “White Oleander”
web_evidence.note: Salon’s contemporary review identifies Astrid as the narrator of the novel’s episodic drama from childhood through age eighteen, including the foster-home sequence and her relationship with Ingrid.

web_evidence.title: White Oleander by Janet Fitch
web_evidence.note: Publishers Weekly’s full-book review identifies Astrid as the narrator and follows her narration across successive foster homes through the concluding choice involving Ingrid’s trial.

search_log: Searched “White Oleander Janet Fitch official excerpt first chapter,” “White Oleander Janet Fitch point of view first person narrator Astrid,” and “White Oleander Janet Fitch excerpt Astrid narration”; opened the permission-reprinted BookBrowse and Bookreporter Chapter 1 excerpts.

Searched “White Oleander first-person Astrid novel,” “White Oleander third-person narration novel,” “White Oleander alternating point of view narrator,” and “White Oleander Astrid narrator Janet Fitch review”; found consistent first-person descriptions and no credible evidence of alternating or third-person base sections.
Opened and checked the University of Delaware thesis, Salon review, Publishers Weekly review, and BookRags point-of-view page before using their claims.

Checked Janet Fitch’s official White Oleander page and Hachette’s title page; both verified the work and Astrid-centered story but lacked explicit narrative-person evidence, so they were not used as person support.
person_note: The Goodreads material repeatedly exposes Astrid as a participating “I” across many distinct scenes, including foster homes, school, Berlin, and reflections on Ingrid. Dialogue and aphorisms were treated as local or nondiagnostic, while generalized “you” was not mistaken for second-person narration. The authorized opening independently confirms the same first-person voice, and whole-book scholarly and professional-review evidence identifies Astrid as the narrator throughout her foster-care journey. Ingrid’s speech, advice, poetry, and reported words are embedded material rather than autonomous base sections. No credible evidence of sustained narration in another person was found; the remaining limitation is that the authorized prose source covers only the opening, but the broad quote coverage and whole-book structural sources resolve that scope limitation.
